Rather, every child and adult is expected to know North Korea's foundational Ten Principles by heart. They state that citizens must hold the "firm perspective" they know of "nothing greater than the great comrades" Kim Il Sung, the founder of North Korea, his son Kim Jong Il and the ruling party. The "smallest attempt" to dent this authority must not be tolerated, it adds.

The report documents both the indoctrination as well as the constant surveillance, with police and a network of neighbourhood spies monitoring suspicious activities. A former police informant says she was instructed to gather information on neighbours' worshipping, and handed a memo by an officer describing Christianity as an "anti-socialist activity".

North Korean authorities are also reported to hold intergenerational records of families' beliefs condemning Christians' children and grandchildren to a life without higher education or decent career prospects.
All of this illustrates how various North Korean institutions, including schools and the police, control its citizens' beliefs from "cradle to the grave," co-author James Burt says.

And yet many North Koreans turn to religion because their lives are so precarious, he adds. Faith offers them something that the state ideology "with its rigid doctrines and disconnect from their lived realities" cannot.

blocks.alt: People pay tribute to the statues of late North Korean leaders Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il at Mansu Hill in Pyongyang on April 15, 2025, to mark the 113th birth anniversary of late leader Kim Il Sung, celebrated as the "Day of the Sun".

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Image caption,
North Koreans pay tribute to statues of the late Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il

Kim Bo-bin grew up in North Hamgyong province, along the border with China. It was a remote, impoverished part of the country where those deemed "untrustworthy" by the state ended up, such as landowners and Christians.

Stuck at the bottom of a state-enforced hierarchy, this "hostile class" had little chance of moving up the ladder. Many of Kim's neighbours were barred from higher education and government positions, or ever living in Pyongyang.

One of them was an exiled "crazy grandma" who used to disappear into a coal shed every morning to chant words 10-year-old Kim didn't recognise. "One day, [the grandma] told me we go from ashes to ashes and dust to dust," she recalls. It was only 12 years later, when she encountered a Bible for the first time in her life that she realised the grandma was a Christian.

When a devastating famine began in the late 1990s, North Hamgyong was one of the first regions to starve because it was cut off from the state's food supply which prioritised Pyongyang. Millions were killed in what the regime described euphemistically as the "Arduous March". It was a time when many North Koreans crossed into China seeking food and work.

Kim was one of them. Aged 22 in 2003, she took what she believed was a job opportunity in China offered by a friend's aunt. But once she crossed the border, she was forced into marriage with a Chinese man and became pregnant.

While picking up a free pram for her newborn daughter at a building adorned with a cross, she encountered a missionary for the first time. Kim would join a growing group of people who discovered Christianity in China - a group that Pyongyang saw as a threat when they were returned to the North, according to Prof Kang.

blocks.alt: This photo taken on November 19, 2017 shows a general view of the city of Chongjin on North Korea's northeast coast.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
A view of the city of Chongjin in North Korea's North Hamgyong province

Kim was arrested in China in 2007 and deported. During interrogation, she says North Korean secret police asked her if she'd ever worn a cross on her neck. She pretended not to understand. She told the police she only recognised the symbol from hospital buildings.

Kim Bo-bin says it was God's blessing the interrogator seemed more interested in whether she intended to flee to South Korea, a grave offence. She says she was beaten for 23 days and sentenced to three years of hard labour at a prison. Her story tallies with multiple accounts in Korea Future's report of extreme police violence causing broken bones and severe bleeding.

Lee Young-joo, who Kim Bo-bin met in prison also after being deported from China, tells the BBC she was interrogated about whether she'd met any missionaries, been to a church or seen a Bible. "Of course you must deny all of it. I said no, I haven't seen it," she told them.
In her prison cell, Lee says she'd keep her eyes open, begging God to save her life. Whenever anyone shut their eyes, guards would swear and shout: "Are you praying?"

Lee is glad she wasn't found to be a Christian, because she says she "would have been sent to a political prisoners' camp. I would be tortured and never allowed to leave and be buried there." This is a widely-held fear among defectors, although Korea Future's report did not hear any first-hand testimonies of Christians being held in such camps.

Lee, who previously shared with the BBC the abuse she suffered inside prison, says she was sentenced to three-and-half years. Outside of hard labour, she would spend time praying, sometimes with other Christian inmates. They would hold hands and whisper Bible verses from memory.

blocks.alt: A photo showing a bespectacled Lee Young-joo staring ahead. She is wearing in pink cardigan over a pink shirt, and a green scarf.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/ Hosu Lee
Image caption,
Lee Young-joo first met a Christian after she escaped from North Korea into China
She and Kim Bo-bin eventually returned home after serving their sentences, where they continued to practise their religion in secret, they tell the BBC.

Kim says she managed to convert her younger sister and other relatives: "My aunt's walls are thick. The neighbours can't hear us so I quietly taught them hymns and about the all-knowing and all-powerful God."

Lee tells the BBC her mother was horrified when she learned of her Christian faith. Undeterred, she told her that she would escape again to join her daughter, who had been left in China as Lee was arrested and deported. When her mother protested, she responded saying they could all live together later.
Her incredulous mother asked: where? "In heaven," she replied.

Today, Lee attends a small church of North Korean escapees in Seoul. She prays daily, to thank God for the chicken soup and the stroll along the river. She prays for her daughter, who escaped with her in 2010, to find a nice Christian man to marry. Her mother died in North Korea some years after her escape, she was told.
Kim managed to flee to South Korea eventually, in 2012, at the age of 30, along with her daughter. She prays throughout the day - and not silently. At church on Sundays, she is the loudest singer.

Commentary: Jensen Huang should never have been too big to fail at Nvidia

Nvidia may be too big to fail. Jensen Huang shouldn’t have been, says Dave Lee for Bloomberg Opinion.

US President Donald Trump presents the National Medal of Science to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the "Golden Age of American Innovation Summit" at the Institute of Peace in Washington, DC, on Oct 8, 2026. (File photo: AFP/Kent Nishimura)

NEW YORK: Nvidia may be too big to fail. Jensen Huang shouldn’t have been.

The chipmaker’s stunning announcement on Monday (Nov 23) morning that it had reinstated Huang as chief executive officer - just a little more than a week after his resignation - carried a telling line: “In the process of reaching its decision, the board received input from senior levels of the United States government.”

And, sure enough, those “senior levels” had a statement ready to go as well. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social.

On Monday, he confirmed he had been speaking to Nvidia’s board directly. “I believe my intervention was very important,” he said.

RISE TO FALL TO RISE AGAIN

The Huang story has now gone from rise, to fall, to rise again. Who can predict what comes next in that sequence?

A US$1 trillion valuation gain in the wake of the news suggests Wall Street’s approval of what it sees as a Nvidia back on track as the linchpin of American AI - its talented, though tainted, talisman again at the helm. That means (it assumes) no pullback in AI spending (though there still might be) and guaranteed future innovations.

“It restores continuity across Nvidia’s product roadmap, customer relationships and supplier partnerships and lowers the leadership risk that drove part of our recent multiple compression,” Citi analyst Atif Malik wrote.

Investors seem unconcerned that Trump, who has a personal investment in Nvidia, has now played kingmaker for two US chip giants: the first was Intel last summer, in the kind of meddling that would have once produced howls of discontent. (And it’s not the first time this year Trump has had a red card rescinded, either.)

They also seemed unconcerned about Huang’s extramarital affairs with subordinates at the company and, of course, one suspected Chinese spy.

Commentary: Jensen Huang’s downfall will accelerate US-China ‘great decoupling’

Commentary: Everything Jensen Huang said about China is out the window

A GRAVE MISTAKE?

Business as usual would be a grave mistake for Nvidia and the broader economy. In the furore around Huang’s actions and subsequent ouster, more has been revealed about the company he built and the governance disaster he presided over.

The 60 direct reports were one significant red flag of a company poorly built. The other is what looks to be an exceedingly lax approach to ensuring his company’s chips didn’t get into the hands of US adversaries. There are congressional appearances to be made - Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec 3 - and an SEC investigation into “accounting practices”, according to a Reuters report last week, that needs to continue to its meticulous conclusion.

Trump’s indifference to Huang’s actions must not change that. A soon-to-be Democrat-led Congress thankfully shows no sign of backing off. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Senator Chuck Schumer posted on X.

The Nvidia board - which has been thoroughly humiliated by this turn of events, even though it’s putting on a united front - stressed its internal investigation would continue. We can be fairly confident its findings won’t rise to the level of costing Huang his job again. The company also mentioned its recently formed “National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks”.

Take that as an acknowledgment that Nvidia, under Huang, was not doing all it could to keep tabs on where its chips were ending up — and there may be significant revenue headwinds when it finds out. And there’s still the small matter of what the suspected Chinese spy might know.

Maybe, to give Huang the benefit of the doubt, all this happened too quickly. Though we speak of Huang as though he saw the future, the more nuanced truth is that he and Nvidia soared because of a fortuitous sequence of events. The company that had set out to design chips that would make video games run better suddenly discovered that those chips were pretty neat for building AI as well. Then the world changed, and Huang became one of the most important people in it.

What if, instead of a string of affairs, Huang had been hit by a bus? Had a heart attack? Contracted deadly food poisoning from street food? Would we now be saying that a US$4 trillion company was about to wither away? That American national security was at grave risk?

If yes, as his reinstatement suggests, then that’s simply untenable, an indictment of the company Huang - who isn’t immortal - was running and will now run again.

Huang’s misdeeds were enough in any sane world for him to have been sacked or at least put on leave until the facts were fully known. But clearly we don’t live in a sane world, so here we are. Huang’s urgent job is to start reorganising Nvidia so it can survive without him.

Nvidia, Anthropic end sharply lower as AI selloff resumes

Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, US, Nov 24, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Brendan McDermid)

FAST

NEW YORK: Nvidia and other tech shares endured another selloff Tuesday (Nov 24) amid lingering questions over the AI boom, giving back some of the bounty from the prior session's rally.

The holiday-shortened week's second trading day followed Monday's shock announcement by Nvidia reinstating CEO Jensen Huang that prompted a ferocious rally in artificial intelligence shares.

But Nvidia, which soared more than 30 per cent on Monday, tumbled almost six per cent on Tuesday.

Fellow tech behemoth and AI giant Anthropic also slumped, giving up 6.5 per cent to US$81.91, below its US$83 price for last week's IPO.

Weakness in semiconductor stocks and AI players like CoreWeave led to a 1.5 per cent drop in the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 finished moderately lower, while the Dow gained.

"We have basically a mixed market," said Peter Cardillo of Spartan Capital.

"The key here is that the Nvidia saga is not causing a rut in the whole market, just a sector of the market," Cardillo said. "We're seeing the old economy stocks, value stocks doing quite nicely."

Nvidia was one of just six equities in the 30-company Dow index to end lower, with Merck, Nike, Amgen and Salesforce all winning more than four per cent.

Monday aside, AI stocks had already sold off sharply throughout November on worries about profitability and the vast sums pumped into the sector.

Huang had resigned less than two weeks ago over extramarital affairs, reportedly with an alleged Chinese spy as well as a senior Nvidia executive before US President Donald Trump successfully pressured the Nvidia board to reverse course.

Jensen Huang is back, but questions facing Nvidia remain, say analysts

Anthropic shares tumble below US$83 IPO price, on track to lose nearly US$200 billion in value

Analysts were in broad agreement that Huang's return did not mean an end to probes or the uncertainty that has clouded the AI trade for six months.

The company remains under scrutiny from investigators including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia's top-line chips.

Europe's main stock markets, which feature far fewer tech companies than their Asian and US rivals, finished a handful of percentage points lower after jumping Monday in line with Wall Street.

Away from the tech sector, French pharmaceutical giant Sanofi revealed it would buy the US biopharma group Insmed, a specialist in respiratory treatments, for US$41 billion as it races to bulk up its development pipeline of new drugs.

Sanofi's share price closed up almost 10 per cent following the news.

Monday's Wall Street surge had propelled Asian markets earlier Tuesday, with Taipei surging nine per cent higher as chip titans TSMC and MediaTek added nearly 10 per cent each.

Seoul piled on more than six per cent thanks to strong gains in fellow chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung, and Tokyo rose nearly four per cent, led by a 12.5-per cent jump for semiconductor tester Advantest.

China's Huawei convicted in sprawling US criminal trial over Iran business

A Brooklyn federal jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 criminal counts over deceiving banks about Iran business and stealing US companies’ trade secrets.

A view shows a Huawei logo at Huawei Technologies France headquarters in Boulogne-Billancourt near Paris, France, January 9, 2025. REUTERS/Gonzalo Fuentes/ File Photo

FAST

NEW YORK: Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei was convicted by a jury in New York City on Tuesday (Nov 25) in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it deceived banks about its business in Iran and stole trade secrets from American companies.

The verdict came in a criminal case that began in 2018, with the US government the following year placing Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology amid American concerns that Huawei posed national security risks.

The jury in Brooklyn federal court found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts the company faced, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets. The jury acquitted Huawei of conspiring to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging the company had acted as a criminal enterprise.

The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defense calling 15. It was not immediately clear what penalties Huawei will face when US District Judge Ann Donnelly sentences it on Sep 14, 2027.

Reuters stories in 2012 and 2013 helped expose Huawei's activities in Iran and were discussed during the trial.

"After the media started questioning Huawei's operations in Iran, so did Huawei's banks," prosecutor Meredith Arfa told jurors during closing arguments in the case last week.

Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, said the company was disappointed by the convictions but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge vindicated its "good-faith compliance culture."

"We fully expect to appeal," Heberlig told reporters.

US Attorney Joseph Nocella said in a statement: “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws.” China's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

US plans to ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers

Asked how much the company may have to pay in penalties, Heberlig said it was premature to comment, but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge could make a significant difference.

Experts have said the case did not undermine Huawei's business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China's push for artificial intelligence.

FOUNDER'S DAUGHTER WAS DETAINED

In December 2018, Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer and daughter of the company's founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the United States, China and Canada.

Meng had been secretly indicted on US charges of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of American sanctions. Meng fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero's welcome. The charges against her were dropped.

Meng did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.

ADEN, Yemen: As Yemen's Houthis push closer towards the temporary capital Aden against fragmented government forces, the city's inhabitants face a bleak choice: stay under fire or leave for an impoverished countryside.

Aden has had no major warfare since bitter street battles of 2015, soon after the internationally recognised government fled Houthi-run Sanaa and made the port city its base, but it is now being hit by missile and drone strikes.

"Rockets are being fired into this city in a frightening way. People are in a state of constant anxiety," said Tariq Abdul Rahman, a former soldier living in Aden with his family.

FRAGMENTED DEFENCE

The Houthis have been on the march on nearly every front since Yemen's civil war reignited this summer after a four-year truce. They are now only 80km (50 miles) from Aden on the front line in the highlands to the north and 110km to the west, along a desert road with few natural obstacles.

Forces inside Aden, perched around an extinct volcano jutting into the Indian Ocean, have set up checkpoints, pulled in reinforcements, dug trenches and set up earth barricades on roads to the front line, residents and military sources say.

But feuding among rival factions, and between their Gulf backers, has undermined the government's efforts to stave off the advance of the Iran-aligned Houthis and now risks hobbling its defence of the city, according to analysts.

"These forces may share a common enemy in the Houthis, but they do not share the same political objectives, territorial priorities, or willingness to fight," said Yemen analyst Mohammed al-Basha, of the UK-based Royal United Services Institute think tank.

Yemen's internationally recognised government said the forces fighting the Houthis were not divided and were working together on the ground.

"Government forces defending Aden operate under a unified strategic command. The Giants Brigades, the Homeland Shield Forces, the Emergency Forces, and units from the Third, Sixth and Seventh Military regions coordinate their efforts," said Emad Bamatraf, deputy head of the Yemeni mission in Washington, in comments emailed after publication.

Saudi skyscraper hit again, coalition slams 'terrorist attack'

Yemen's Houthis say Saudi attack kills 17

As soldiers stood at a checkpoint in Aden this week, monitoring or searching cars, the only flags they displayed belonged to the former state of South Yemen that unified with the north in 1990.

Those flags - ubiquitous in Aden - show the southern groups' eventual goal of reversing unification. But big differences between those groups have flared into violence.

Last winter factions backed by Saudi Arabia and the Southern Transitional Council, supported by the United Arab Emirates, spent weeks battling each other for control of territory. It ended with the UAE pulling out of the military coalition fighting the Houthis and a Saudi-backed faction splitting off from the STC while the movement's leadership quit government.

The STC has not taken part in the latest fighting against the Houthis, though it vows it will defend Aden and the south if needed. Other southern factions have refused to fight for territory in the former state of north Yemen.

"On the ground we coordinate with others to defend the south and that will continue," said STC spokesperson Anwar al-Tamimi, while criticising the effectiveness of government efforts to impose a clear command and control on the anti-Houthi forces.

However, the STC's political demands - including a referendum on southern secession - must be addressed, he added.

"What we won't do is send our soldiers into an offensive with no strategy and no route to a political settlement," he said.

ANXIETY ON THE STREETS

Inside Aden, Abdul Rahman has trouble sleeping at night, he said, sometimes torn awake by the blast of a missile hitting the city and on other nights lying restlessly fretting about his family's future in a poor, war-stricken land.

"Shells are falling randomly on streets, markets, and homes. This terrifies people so much," said Abdul Rahman, who spent 30 years in the military and now lives with his family of nine in a humble three-room house.

"People worry about their children, the women, and children at home ... What's destined to be? What will tomorrow bring?"

Fears of war have added to the gnawing anxiety Abdul Rahman said he already faced over money in a city where state salaries barely cover living expenses.

He already owes money to local shops, he said, and while he is glad they are willing to extend him credit, he feels constantly guilty about those rising debts.

With the war drawing closer to the city again, he says the family's distress has deepened and brought a stark choice.

"I don't know if I should stay in the city, or try to return to the countryside," he said. He has no answer, he added, believing the future bleak in either case, and is not even sure the family could afford a fare out.

Hundreds of thousands of people have already been displaced since Yemen's war began again, with many now surviving on meagre aid handouts in small tarpaulin camps in the hills around Taiz, Yemen's third largest city, now besieged by the Houthis.

Khaled Abdo, a day labourer on construction sites in Aden, has 10 children and barely enough work to get by. He has not worked for more than a week, he said.

The danger from the Houthis has only added to his woes. "We want security and stability and Yemen to go back to being a state, the way we used to live before," he said.

PARIS: France's ex-president Nicolas Sarkozy, his wife singer Carla Bruni and a paparazzi boss will stand trial next year over alleged witness tampering in a case over funding for his 2007 election, a source close to the case said Tuesday (Nov 24).

France's right-wing leader from 2007 to 2012 has been embroiled in legal woes since leaving office.

Last year he became modern France's first former president to go to jail over seeking illegal campaign funding from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi in exchange for help restoring his international image.

The former head of state was freed from jail after 20 days pending his appeal, and an appeals court is to issue its ruling on Monday.

One of the main accusers in the case was French-Lebanese businessman Ziad Takieddine, who died in Lebanon last year.

In 2016 he claimed he helped deliver up to five million euros (US$6 million) in cash from Kadhafi to Sarkozy and the former president's chief of staff in 2006 and 2007.

But in November 2020, Takieddine suddenly retracted his incriminating statement in an interview with French media.

He later returned to his initial claims.

This prompted accusations that Sarkozy and his wife enlisted the help of paparazzi queen Mimi Marchand to pay the witness to change his mind, something they have always denied.

Bruni is suspected of having requested a clandestine phone line in late 2019 to communicate with Marchand about the Takieddine operation.

A court will in November next year try Sarkozy and Bruni on charges of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" as well as benefiting from witness tampering, the source told AFP.

Marchand stands accused of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" as well as witness tampering.

Their lawyers did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.

The defendants face a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a fine of 150,000 euros.

Sarkozy has received two definitive convictions in other cases - linked to overspending in his failed 2012 re-election bid, and later trying to extract favours from a judge.

Marchand was last year handed an 18-month suspended prison sentence for blackmailing a television host, who feared the paparazzi boss would publish images of her daughter leaving police custody.

French protesters bear scars of police violence

French riot police apprehend a protester amid clashes during demonstration organised by labour unions in Paris as part of nationwide protests, in France, Oct 24, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Abdul Saboor)

PARIS: Police in France have seriously injured dozens of protesters since student demonstrations grew into a wider movement, according to an AFP tally based on first-hand accounts, victims' lawyers and NGO records.

At least 31 people have been seriously injured by security forces since the protests began in September, 16 of them suffering permanent damage to an eye or the loss of a limb, according to the tally.

Authorities have not provided an official count of demonstrators injured, but by early November, France's internal police investigation service had opened more than 140 probes into alleged police brutality.

Rights groups have accused law enforcement of using unjustified force in charging crowds with batons and firing crowd-control grenades at demonstrators at close range.

But the interior ministry has said policing has been legal and proportionate.

AFP spoke to three demonstrators who were injured:

PRANNY OUCH, MAIMED LEG

Clinging to her walker, 25-year-old Pranny Ouch made her way to a brown leather couch to rest her injured leg.

The art student, "not particularly an activist", travelled from a Paris suburb to join protests on Oct 17, feeling "a lot of hope" on a day that descended into some of the worst rioting France has seen in years.

She said she was "just passing through" the Republique square amid tear gas when she was struck in the leg by what she and her lawyer believe was part of a tear gas canister.

The impact caused an open fracture of both lower leg bones and a gaping wound, requiring three operations and several skin and tissue grafts.

An external fixator now holds 15 pins in place from her foot to just below her knee.

The daughter of a political refugee who fled Cambodia's Khmer Rouge regime, Ouch said she had always "idealised" France.

"I never expected to experience this one day in France," she said.

"I don't understand how anyone could hurl such violent weapons at people who simply want to express an opinion," she added, breaking down in tears.

"How do we rebuild our lives?"

A picture of Rémi Aubert and an X-ray of his injuries during an interview in Marseille on Nov 20, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Miguel Medina)

REMI AUBERT, "SPITTING BLOOD"

Remi Aubert, a 39-year-old podiatrist, has struggled to speak since police struck him in the face with batons in Marseille on Oct 31, knocking out his teeth and breaking his nose.

Aubert said he had left the protest and was emerging from a restaurant when an officer struck him with a baton and another threw him to the ground.

"There were baton blows and kicks to the face. I was spitting blood," he said.

He had eight teeth knocked out or broken, leaving him with a 20,000-euro (US$22,000) bill for repairs.

Aubert said he suffers from nightmares and other symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder.

But he has returned to protesting, still focused on "social and economic demands" while also denouncing police brutality.

"I'm speaking out so that police violence stops. To show that these aren't just a few isolated cases," he said.

France workers strike, march for 'dignified wage'

French protesters rally for sixth weekend over living costs, public services

STUN AND TEAR GAS GRENADE

A 21-year-old woman, who asked not to be named after online threats, has a machine connected to her leg to prevent the tissue from dying.

Saudi skyscraper hit again, coalition slams 'terrorist attack'

Saudi Arabia's civil defence later said 11 people were injured in the attack it blamed on the Houthis.

View of the damage to the Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, following a Houthi attack in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Nov 19, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Saudi Press Agency)

RIYADH: The Saudi capital's tallest skyscraper was struck for the second time in days on Tuesday (Nov 24), witnesses said, injuring 11 people, as the coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis denounced a "terrorist attack".

Three separate witnesses said the strike targeted the 80-storey Public Investment Fund Tower, which houses the kingdom's sovereign wealth fund and dominates Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD).

The building, which was also attacked last Thursday, is one of several high-profile targets hit since hostilities with the Iran-backed Houthis restarted in July.

"One of the towers in the financial centre was targeted in a cowardly terrorist attack," coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said in a social media post, without naming the building.

"The relevant authorities are currently inspecting the attack site."

Saudi Arabia's civil defence later said 11 people were injured in the attack it blamed on the Houthis.

"The attack resulted in 11 people being injured," read a report by the Saudi Press Agency, saying Indian, Nepali and Egyptian nationals along with Saudi citizens were among those wounded.

A source briefed on the details of the attack told AFP that several people were in the tower repairing the damage caused by last week's attack when the building was struck again Tuesday.

The source said at least two of the 11 injured were in critical condition after sustaining severe burns during the strike.

An attack on the PIF is symbolic as the fund is driving efforts to diversify the oil-reliant Saudi economy - a project that has been complicated by the Middle East war and Houthi strikes.

A tower belonging to state oil giant Aramco in KAFD was hit earlier this month, while Riyadh's international airport was repeatedly struck in October with one attack killing 14 people.

A fourth witness told AFP a vehicle fitted with a speaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover on Tuesday. No warning was sent to mobile phones about any threats to the capital.

Afterwards, police cars blocked some entrances to the gleaming financial district, a showpiece of Saudi Arabia's modernisation under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto ruler.

A waiter at a KAFD restaurant told AFP: "We just reopened a while ago.

"They evacuated all of us telling us a tower has been hit. They closed the streets and they banned people from passing in streets or entering."

WEEKS OF VIOLENCE

Last week, Saudi officials said an attack on a tower in the financial district damaged several floors and two adjacent buildings but caused no casualties.

Although authorities did not identify the building, photos released by the civil defence agency appeared to show shattered glass and other exterior damage to the PIF tower.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for last week's attack, but they did not announce any fresh attacks on Tuesday.

Standing 385 metres high, the PIF tower is the most prominent landmark of KAFD, a showcase for Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions.

With imposing skyscrapers, luxury shops and green spaces, the district also hosts the headquarters of the Saudi stock exchange along with multinationals such as Goldman Sachs.

The Houthis have stepped up their attacks against Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, striking military, civilian and oil infrastructure.

The major attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport forced the suspension of flights for two weeks. Several events have been cancelled, including the Future Investment Initiative financial conference, dubbed "Davos in the desert".

In response, a Saudi-led military coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen's government has been striking Houthi targets in the impoverished country.

Saudi Arabia says it intercepts three Houthi missiles targeting Riyadh

Yemen's Houthis say Saudi attack kills 17

On Tuesday, local officials said a coalition airstrike on buses and trucks killed 26 people in Lahj province. Government forces blamed the Houthis for the attack.

As the conflict shows no sign of slowing, Britain sanctioned the Houthis and four of its top officials "for deliberately attempting to undermine stability" on Tuesday.

The measures include an asset freeze against the group and an asset freeze and travel ban on four figures, including security and intelligence head Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani, and interior affairs official Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi.

The Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in early 2015, after the Houthis had captured the capital Sanaa and sent the internationally recognised government fleeing to Aden.

The war left hundreds of thousands dead and triggered a humanitarian catastrophe before an uneasy ceasefire went into effect in 2022.

Source: AFP/fs

items.title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
items.summary: Naeem Abu Nahel, who had been in the post for two months, is among seven Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes on Tuesday.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

A funeral was held earlier in southern Gaza for three Palestinians killed in an Israeli strike

ByDavid Gritten

Updated 37 minutes ago

At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.

Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.

The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.

Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.

Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.

The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.

Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.

Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.

The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".

It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".

Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Gaza's health ministry warned that there was a rapid rise in cases of meningitis in October

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.

The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.

The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.

On Tuesday, the health ministry warned that there had been a rapid rise in cases of meningitis, with 272 reported in October - about eight times the usual monthly average.

Fifteen deaths had been attributed to the infection so far this year, including five reported between August and October, it said.

Israeli military body Cogat said on Monday it was "working to provide a dedicated humanitarian response" and that a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment had been presented at a meeting with UN agencies.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Watch: Moment troops raid home and capture Mexican drug lord

Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops entered a house and detained a Mexican drug lord who had managed to evade capture for years.

The video shows armed personnel entering via a garage and finding Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as 'El Chapo Isidro', who was on the FBI's most wanted list.

Seven suspects were killed in last Friday's operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

The arrest of Meza Flores in the northern Sinaloa state sparked a wave of unrest, which led to eight alleged drug cartel members being detained for their involvement in the retaliatory violence.

Cheers and applause as Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia office

Cheers and applause as Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia office

Nvidia's board unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and president on Monday. President Trump has claimed credit for brokering the deal.

What is the mood at Nvidia following the announcement? BBC's Lily Jamali reports from Nvidia's headquarters, where she gauges the reaction to Huang's return.
